Thanks for the time this morning — quick recap and a few clarifying questions so we can size the demo and trial correctly.

Summary of what I heard:
- Primary app: FinApps customer-facing financial assistant (chat + structured summaries).
- Typical interaction: short user query + 1-2 system prompts (templates), variable user text length.
- Key ask: show cost under realistic load and confirm what caching / prefix reuse does to billed units.

Questions / requests (would appreciate short answers where possible):
1) Monthly scale: please confirm expected monthly active users and an estimated monthly token volume (ballpark is fine).
2) Average prompt size: can you share a sample of the typical user prompt (we only need a de-identified row) and typical system prompt lengths (chars or tokens).
3) Cache pattern: you said many system prompts are identical — what percent of requests do you expect to be exact-match cache hits (e.g., 20%, 50%, 80%)?
4) Budget anchor: you mentioned targeting around $/1M tokens — what range should I assume for procurement (e.g., $100–$200 / 1M tokens)?
5) SLO constraints: what latency tail matters (p50/p95 target)? this affects batch vs single-token optimizations.

Attachments: I uploaded a tiny CSV (finapps-usage-sample.csv) with three anonymized rows to give us a starting point for a cost estimate (tokens/char column included). Also attaching a short pricing anchor doc so the legal/proc team has context.

Next steps I propose:
- Your replies to the 5 items above -> I’ll send a quick calculator and an estimate showing sample unit economics at 3 volume tiers (100k / 1M / 5M monthly tokens).
- Optional: 30-minute tech check next week (Karthik + Monica will join to validate caching behavior and logging).

Thanks — talk soon,

Thanks Aisha — great summary. Answers inline below.

1) Monthly scale: currently ~12k MAUs for the pilot cohort. Expect to ramp to ~60k MAUs over 6 months. Ballpark token volume: pilot ~400k tokens/month, ramp target ~4–6M tokens/month.

2) Prompt sizes: user queries average ~40–120 characters (short, often single-line). System prompts (templates + instructions) are ~600–1,200 characters. I attached a short export of 2 real example prompts (de-identified).

3) Cache pattern: system prompts are identical for ~70% of calls. But user queries vary, so full-response cache hits (exact same user+system) are rare (~5%). We were thinking prefix caching could help a lot if supported (i.e., reuse of system prompt + partial user prefix).

4) Budget anchor: procurement is targeting roughly $125–$175 / 1M tokens for hosted inference. If we can get to the low end via caching/quantization, procurement will be happy.

5) Latency SLOs: p95 should be under 700ms for interactive UI (desktop/web), p99 is less strict but would prefer under 1.5s.

A couple of clarifying questions for you: does Redwood bill on tokens or characters for the hosted API? And how does cache hit accounting work — will a full cache hit avoid token billing entirely or is there a small retrieval charge?

Happy to jump on the tech check next week — Tue or Thu mornings ET work for us.

Subject: Re: Billing units & prompt-cache impact — anchoring on $/1M tokens

Hi Samir — perfect, thanks for the details. Quick answers and an operational note so procurement is comfortable.

Short answers:
- Redwood bills on tokens (not raw characters). For English, a rough rule of thumb is ~3.5–4 characters per token (this varies by language and punctuation).
- Billing counts \"model tokens\": the input tokens we send to the model + the output tokens generated.
- Caching behavior (how it affects billing):
  * Full-response cache hit (we return a stored model response without running the model) => no model-inference tokens billed. That reduces billed tokens to zero for that request (aside from a tiny metadata retrieval cost).
  * Prefix/system-prompt caching (we cache parts like system prompt and associated KV-cache states) => if we can serve the cached prefix and only run the model for the fresh suffix, billed tokens correspond only to the portion actually sent to and produced by the model. In practice this means substantial savings when system prompts are large and user input is small.
  * Partial-match or similarity caches may still require a short model run to adapt; billed tokens reflect the run.

Operational note for procurement: full cache hits remove model compute and therefore the bulk of token billing, but teams should plan for a conservative baseline assuming no cache (i.e., worst-case billed tokens = input+output for every request). Then show two scenarios in the cost model: 1) conservative (no cache), 2) realistic (use your 70% system-prompt reuse and 5% full-hit numbers to estimate savings).

Quick example using your numbers:
- System prompt: 900 chars -> ~225 tokens (approx).
- User query: 80 chars -> ~20 tokens.
- If model generates 120 tokens on average: billed tokens/no-cache = 225+20+120 = 365 tokens per request.
- If we can cache the 225-token system prompt and get a cache hit for that portion: billed tokens/cache = 20+120 = 140 tokens (62% reduction).

Economics: at your procurement anchor ($125 / 1M tokens):
- No-cache cost per 1M requests (at 365 tokens/request) -> ~365M tokens -> cost = (365M / 1M) * $125 = $45,625 for 1M requests.
- With 70% system-prompt reuse (as you said), effective tokens/request shifts toward the cached case for many requests — I’ll run the calculator and show per-tier costs.

Next steps I’ll take this afternoon:
1) Create a short calc (100k / 1M / 5M tiers) using your pilot/ramp numbers and both conservative + cache-adjusted scenarios.
2) Karthik or Monica will join the tech check to validate the caching pattern and logs (we can show request-level trace and exactly which tokens were billed in our sandbox).
3) If the numbers look good, I’ll draft a short trial SOW that includes a caching-enabled sandbox and telemetry so procurement can verify billed tokens during POC.

Proposed times for tech check: Tue 10/06 at 11:00 AM ET or Thu 10/08 at 9:00 AM ET — which is better for you?

Thanks — I’ll attach the calc and a short one-pager for procurement once I put the numbers together.
